item.title: Lucy mission to Trojan asteroids: 5 years of discoveries - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
• NASA’s Lucy mission is headed to the Trojan asteroids. These asteroids, traveling ahead of and behind Jupiter in its orbit, have never been explored before.
  • Lucy is now less than a year away from the Trojans. But it has already made several exciting discoveries.
  • These include new findings at other asteroids in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter.

5 years into the Lucy mission

NASA’s Lucy spacecraft is getting ever closer to its destination, the Trojan asteroids. These are two groups of asteroids that travel ahead of and behind Jupiter in its orbit. Lucy is now less than a year away from meeting its first Trojan. Exciting!

Launched on October 16, 2021, Lucy has been traveling for about five years now. But even though it hasn’t reached the asteroids yet, it has already made several remarkable discoveries, researchers from the Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) said on October 19, 2026.

An ambitious mission to unexplored asteroids

Lucy will be the first mission to explore the Trojan asteroids. Hal Levison at SwRI is the principal investigator of the mission. He said:

Lucy is an ambitious NASA mission, with plans to visit 11 asteroids in its 12-year mission to tour the Trojan asteroids that are located in two swarms leading and trailing Jupiter. As we passed through the main asteroid belt, we visited three asteroids, capturing close-up views of those bodies while performing engineering tests of the spacecraft’s innovative navigation system in advance of the main event to study the Trojans. These relics are effectively fossils of the planet formation process, holding vital clues to deciphering the history of our solar system.

Dinkinesh has a moon

Even though Lucy hasn’t reached the Trojans yet, it has already made several discoveries.

The first was at the asteroid Dinkinesh. Back in 2022, the mission team found that Lucy would come close to the asteroid, which was still unnamed at the time. Dinkinesh is in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

The flyby happened in November 2023. The mission team tweaked the spacecraft’s trajectory so it would fly even closer to Dinkinesh. And there was a surprise waiting for them.

The asteroid had a tiny moon! So now, scientists count that as being two asteroids. But there was yet another surprise.

The little moon, now named Selam, was a contact binary. That is, it had two parts that were joined together. So there were three bodies altogether, not just one.

Peanut-shaped Donaldjohanson

Later, in 2025, Lucy flew past another asteroid, Donaldjohanson. And this time, it was the asteroid itself that was a contact binary.

Donaldjohanson is peanut-shaped, with two large lobes joined together by a smooth “neck.” Simone Marchi, deputy principal investigator for Lucy, said:

The Donaldjohanson flyby revealed many surprises about the small asteroid. For instance, the peanut-shaped, two-lobed structure is connected by a remarkably smooth neck. The asteroid also wobbles, rotating end-over-end once every 10.5 Earth days while rolling around its lateral axis once every 26.5 days.

Gravity assists boot Lucy’s speed

During its journey, Lucy looped back and passed by Earth twice. Why? It might sound counterproductive, but the spacecraft uses Earth’s gravity to gain speed and fine-tune its trajectory.

The first gravity assist was in October 2022. Lucy passed only 220 miles (350 km) above the surface of Earth. This propelled Lucy into a two-year solar orbit. Lucy took images of Earth and the moon to calibrate its instruments.

Later, in December 2024, the second flyby increased its speed relative to the sun by over 16,000 mph (25,750 km/h). That put Lucy on a current path to make its first Trojan encounter in August 2027.

Lucy will make yet another Earth flyby in December 2030. It will then reach the second Trojan swarm of asteroids in March 2033.

When problems arise

With any mission, there can be problems that occur, and Lucy was no exception. Soon after launch, one of its two huge solar panels didn’t deploy properly.

However, mission engineers were able to diagnose the problem and get the solar panel to deploy far enough to save the mission.

Other observations

Lucy has been fortunate to witness some other events too during its journey.

In September 2022, NASA DART probe impacted the near-Earth asteroid Didymos (on purpose, to demonstrate planetary defense technology). And Lucy saw it happen.

In September 2025, Lucy observed the now-famous interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS as it passed through our solar system. 

But there is much more to come, as Levison noted:

Despite these eventful five years, most of Lucy’s mission still lies ahead. The main events start in less than a year as Lucy gets a close-up look at four Trojan asteroid systems: Eurybates and its satellite Queta in August 2027, Polymele and its as-yet-unnamed satellite in September 2027, Leucus in April 2028 and Orus in November 2028.

It will be exciting when Lucy finally reaches the Trojans. None of them have been seen up close before, so what will Lucy find?

Bottom line: NASA’s Lucy mission is now less than a year from reaching the Trojan asteroids near Jupiter. And it has already made some exciting discoveries along the way.

item.title: Surprising colors of white dwarf stars revealed for 1st time - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
• White dwarf stars are known to be, well, white. But that might not always be the case.
  • White dwarfs come in a variety of colors, a new study from researchers in the U.K. shows.
  • There are even green white dwarfs. No green stars of any kind have been identified before.

Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter.

What are the true colors of white dwarf stars?

White dwarf stars are white. But is that always the case? It seems that white dwarfs can actually come in a variety of colors. Researchers at the University of Warwick in the U.K. said on October 15, 2026, that white dwarfs can glow in pink, cyan, yellow, purple and green.

Green is the most surprising, since astronomers have never observed any green stars of any kind. Orange, white and blue are the typical colors of stars we see in the night sky.

White dwarfs don’t shine like typical stars, by the way. They’re the hot, dense cores left over when stars run out of fuel and blow their gases into space. Our own sun will become a white dwarf one day. And now we get to wonder … what color will it be?

The researchers published their peer-reviewed findings in RAS Techniques and Instruments on October 15, 2026.

Density determines the colors of white dwarf stars

Mark Hollands, at the University of Warwick, led the new study. He said:

Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like perfect radiators, so their color is set almost entirely by temperature. But nobody had really looked into what else might be possible for white dwarfs. It turns out these incredibly dense stars can produce colors nobody expected, and some of them genuinely surprised me.

So why do white dwarfs come in these varieties of color? It all has to do with the density of the star. The coolest white dwarfs have the highest densities, around 0.036 pounds per cubic inch (1 gram per cubic centimeter). That’s millions of times denser than our sun’s photosphere (its visual surface).

This causes trace elements in the white dwarfs — such as carbon, calcium and sodium — to interact with the dense helium plasma. And they do so across a wide range of colors, wider than in less dense white dwarfs.

Astronomers can’t observe these colors directly. So the researchers used data astronomers already had. This is the spectrum of the white dwarfs, when their light is split into different wavelengths. Then, the researchers used a model of human color vision. That showed what each star would look like if viewed up close with the human eye.

Rainbow colors of white dwarf stars

The results revealed a wide range of colors. Indeed, white dwarfs were far from being just white. This also depended on what was in the atmospheres of the white dwarfs.

The colors fell into two distinct groups. The first group is carbon-rich white dwarfs. They tend to be pink or purple in color.

However, white dwarfs with atmospheres polluted by debris from asteroids or comets tend to be more yellow.

Meanwhile, white dwarfs that have hydrogen and helium atmospheres are more cyan or blue. This is due to hydrogen molecules colliding with helium atoms in their atmospheres.

1st known green star

One of the biggest surprises involved the white dwarf WD J1330+6435. It is the first documented green star. Astronomers have been on the lookout for green stars, but never confirmed one, until now.

Why is it green? As noted before, it has to do with its density and temperature, and the elements in its atmosphere. Calcium, lithium and sodium give it an overall chartreuse green appearance. Hollands said:

The traces of sodium in the atmosphere of this white dwarf absorb the orange part of the spectrum, leaving behind a ghostly green glow. Imagine standing on a planet and looking up at a green star. It feels like something out of science fiction.

Reddest star ever seen?

Red stars are common. In fact, red dwarfs are the most common stars in our galaxy. But now, the researchers might have identified the reddest star ever seen so far.

White dwarf WD J1011+2845 is 48 light-years from Earth. Why is it so red?

The white dwarf has a deep convection zone on the inside, where carbon is brought to the surface from deep below. Incredibly, the carbon molecules distort the star’s light so much that almost all of it is squeezed into wavelengths beyond 600 nanometers. This produces a deep salmon-pink glow unlike anything seen in an ordinary star, even a red dwarf.

Not all white dwarfs are colorful

Does this mean that all white dwarfs are colorful? No. Most of them are still white. The researchers also looked at a more representative sample of white dwarfs, within 65 light-years of Earth. Of the 151 white dwarfs studied, just five displayed the unique coloring.

Three of those stars were pink and two were yellow.

As for the remaining white dwarfs, the medium color temperature was about 6,800 Kelvin (6500 C or 11,700 F). That looks white to the human eye.

This also shows that most white dwarfs are not typically blue, as is often thought. Hotter, bluer white dwarfs are over-represented in surveys, as they can be seen from farther away.

2-faced white dwarf star

While not a colorful white dwarf, astronomers also said in 2023 that they found a white dwarf, nicknamed Janus, that has two different faces. One side of the star is composed of hydrogen, while the other side is helium. The helium side appears more mottled or bubbly, while the hydrogen side is brighter.

Bottom line: Astronomers in the U.K. have found that the true colors of white dwarf stars can vary greatly. They even found the 1st known green star.

Source: Any colour you like: the diverse chromaticities of white dwarfs

Via University of Warwick

item.title: Euclid was mapping the universe. Then it found a comet - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Euclid makes an accidental comet discovery

ESA’s Euclid space telescope is surveying the cosmos, mapping the large-scale structure of the universe in space and time. Its goal is to observe more than 1/3 of the sky, concentrating on how galaxies have evolved over time, in the hopes of providing insight to the nature of dark matter and dark energy. But ESA said on October 19, 2026, that Euclid has made an unexpected discovery, and a first for the space telescope. It spotted a comet some 800 million miles (1.3 billion km) away in our solar system.

The Minor Planet Center named the comet C/2026 S1 (Euclid) in honor of the space telescope. The comet lies somewhere between Jupiter and Saturn’s orbits. Only it’s not in the plane of our solar system with the other planets, asteroids and comets at all. Instead, it’s approximately straight up from the sun’s perspective.

Euclid caught the comet whizzing by background galaxies. Despite its high rate of speed, the comet will still take thousands of years to complete one orbit of the sun.

Finding the streaking fuzzy cloud

Mikko Pöntinen of the University of Helsinki discovered the comet using object-detection software. Pöntinen said:

I was excited to see my software flag a ‘streak’ smeared across several images — the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas.

The space telescope was imaging the Euclid Deep Field North at the time of capture. In the image above, you can see the background galaxies in the field of view as the comet suddenly streaks by. Euclid took those images between September 16 and 24, 2026. The Minor Planet Center confirmed the discovery of the new comet on October 8, 2026.

Euclid intentionally looks away from the solar system’s plane to reduce glare from dust leftover from the creation of planets and asteroids.

Bruno Altieri, Euclid archive scientist and part of the discovery team, said:

Very few comets are expected to be discovered by Euclid so it was a happy coincidence that the combination of the comet’s orbit and Euclid’s scanning over those days captured the object in multiple images.

Finding future targets of the Comet Interceptor

ESA is planning a future mission called Comet Interceptor. The mission will park itself in space and await a target that is not from the plane of our solar system, but one that is pristine and untouched from the outer reaches of the sun’s realm. And now, researchers think Euclid could help Comet Interceptor find a comet to target.

Valeria Pettorino, Euclid project scientist, said:

While this particular comet is not a suitable candidate for Comet Interceptor, the process of discovery and alert gives us a real test case for how our two mission teams will coordinate in the future. And we are of course happy to have discovered a previously unknown comet for the solar system community to follow-up on.

Bottom line: The Euclid space telescope made an accidental comet discovery as it searched the universe for evidence of dark matter and dark energy. The comet is now named C/2026 S1 (Euclid).

item.title: New clues to how infectious fungus Candida auris resists antifungals - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
The fungus Candida auris has spread to more than 60 countries. It’s a growing concern because it can cause serious infections in already hospitalized patients. Now, researchers at the University of Exeter and City St George’s, University of London, have discovered mechanisms that help explain how the fungus survives certain antifungal treatments. The findings could help guide the development of new strategies to combat this pathogen.

The researchers published their peer-reviewed study in the journal Nature Communications on October 15, 2026.

A fungus that is difficult to eliminate

First identified in 2008, Candida auris has become a global public health concern. It can live on the skin and persist on surfaces and medical equipment, making it easier to spread in hospitals. Those most at risk are people who are already seriously ill, particularly patients in intensive care units. If the fungus enters the bloodstream, the infection can be fatal.

But controlling it is not always easy. Some infections persist despite treatment, even when initial laboratory tests suggest that the fungus should respond to the medication.

To understand why this happens, the researchers studied how Candida auris responds to echinocandins, a class of antifungal drugs used to treat serious infections. These drugs work by weakening the fungal cell wall.

Fungus Candida auris changes its cell wall to resist treatment

During one experiment, a researcher accidentally left some samples incubating longer than intended. When the researcher returned to examine them, they found something unexpected: some cells had survived the treatment and started growing again.

One mechanism that could explain how these cells survived involves the cell wall, the structure that protects the fungus. Echinocandins work by blocking an enzyme the fungus needs to produce beta-glucan, one of the main components of its cell wall. By interfering with its production, the drugs weaken the structure that protects the cells.

However, the researchers observed that Candida auris responded by changing the composition of its cell wall. The fungus increased the amount of chitin, another component of the wall, and thickened its inner layer.

By increasing chitin levels and thickening this inner layer, the fungus may be able to compensate for some of the weakening caused by the disruption of beta-glucan production.

Genetic changes help the fungus adapt

In addition to modifying its cell wall, the researchers discovered that Candida auris had extra copies of certain sections of its genetic material. Having multiple copies may allow changes to occur in one of them. If one of these changes helps the fungus resist the antifungal drug, the cells carrying it may be more likely to survive and multiply.

To better understand how these findings relate to drug resistance, the researchers compared the cells that had survived treatment. They found that some formed small colonies and grew slowly, while others formed larger colonies and grew more quickly.

Different populations respond differently to treatment

Although both populations showed resistance to the antifungal drug and shared changes in their cell walls, the researchers found differences in their genetic material.

The cells that formed larger colonies and grew faster had accumulated more changes in a gene involved in the stress response and the maintenance of the cell wall. These changes were associated with even greater resistance to the antifungal drug.

The findings suggest a possible progression: changes in the cell wall may help the fungus withstand the initial effects of treatment, while the accumulation of certain genetic changes may contribute to the emergence of cells that can resist the drug more effectively and grow faster.

New clues for fighting the fungus Candida auris

Although Candida auris remains a significant challenge, learning more about how it resists antifungal drugs is an important step toward combating it. These findings open up new avenues for research and could help guide the development of more effective treatments.

The research team is already investigating combinations of antifungal drugs in the hope of using this knowledge to find new ways to fight the fungus.

Bottom line: Scientists have identified new resistance mechanisms used by the fungus Candida auris, paving the way for advances in antifungal treatments.

Source: FKS1/2-variant independent mechanisms underlying the emergence of resistance in echinocandin-refractory Candida auris infections.

item.title: New dinosaur species identified from fossil stashed in drawer for a century - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
You deserve a daily dose of good news. For the latest in science and the night sky, subscribe to EarthSky’s free daily newsletter.

More than 100 years ago on the Isle of Wight, off the south coast of England, amateur paleontologist Reginald Walter Tooley found a dinosaur fossil. And, in 1924 — after Tooley’s death — the fossil came to the Natural History Museum in London. It was one of a batch of some 1,000 unstudied specimens. The fossil then sat in a drawer for a century. No one knew it would bring to light a new dinosaur species.

Fast forward 100 years. Two paleontologists — Cassius Morrison and his student Charlie Scherer of University College London Earth Sciences — pulled the long-overlooked specimen out of storage. They wondered if it could be reevaluated using modern diagnostic techniques.

The researchers used CT scanning to get a better understanding of the fossil. And they used 3D modeling to show what this dinosaur would have been like when it roamed what’s now the Isle of Wight some 120 million years ago.

They published their peer-reviewed research in the journal Royal Society Open Science on October 14, 2026. They said they’d named this newly recognized dinosaur species Invictibellatrix amberina.

Morrison commented:

It’s a real mystery that this fossil was overlooked for so long, sitting in a drawer for nearly 100 years. Lots of bones are found on the Isle of Wight. Who knows what else is waiting to be discovered.

What’s in a name?

The word amberina primarily honors the amber embedded within the plant debris beds of the Wessex Formation on the Isle of Wight, where the 120-million-year-old fossil was originally collected.

Invictibellatrix, meanwhle, translates from Latin as unconquered female warrior.

The researchers said this dinosaur would have been about as tall as a human. It stood on two legs, ate meat, and likely had feathers, they said.  It would have used its arms and giant claws to attack smaller prey. such as smaller dinos, lizards and mammals.

They found that the skull has an oval hole where the brain and spinal cord would have met. The hour-glass-shaped crest was also distinctive; this crest was what led to the classification as a new species.

It might have been gigantic, but wasn’t

The new dinosaur species belonged to a group of two-legged dinos called the megaraptorans. A species of megaraptoran had never been discovered to exist in Europe until now.

Megaraptorans could be gigantic, as big as a T-rex. But the new human-sized dinosaur is the smallest megaraptoran yet found. While it would have stood around the height of a human, at about 5 feet (1.5 meters), it would have been long from its head to its tail, spanning about 10-13 feet (3-4 meters). And those large, curved claws were likely around 4-8 inches (10-20 cm). These estimates are based on what we know of Invictibellatrix‘s closest relatives, the scientists said.

Cassius Morrison said:

It would have eaten small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals, occupying a similar role in the food chain to the hyena today.

And while humans didn’t yet exist while Invictibellatrix was on Earth, Morrison said:

It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex. We would have been perfectly sized prey, about 1/3 of their body weight. They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small.

Where might the new dinosaur species have lived?

Invictibellatrix amberina is the first member of the megaraptoran family known to live in Europe. Researchers think megaraptorans originated in Asia. Later, they traveled through Europe. The larger carnivorous species became apex predators in areas of what is today Africa, South America and Antarctica. Scherer commented:

This new species is the first proof we have that megaraptorans were also present in Europe and that they reached Gondwana this way rather than island-hopping further south.

The larger megaraptorans came later and lived farther south. Researchers think the smaller megaraptorans who lived farther north died out earlier.

Bottom line: Researchers have identified a new dinosaur species from a fossil found on Isle of Wight in the U.K. The carnivorous dino would have stood about as tall as a human.

Source: A new megaraptoran dinosaur from the Lower Cretaceous Wessex Formation, UK, and its implications for theropod evolution and biogeography

Comet Halley visited last in 1986

The famous comet 1P/Halley – aka Comet Halley – swings into the inner solar system about every 76 years. At such times, the sun’s heat causes the comet to lose its icy grip over its mountain-sized conglomeration of ice, dust, and gas. And so, at each pass, the crumbly comet sheds a fresh trail of debris into its orbital stream. It lost about 1/1,000 of its mass during its last flyby, in 1986.

And it so happens we intersect Comet Halley’s orbit not once, but twice each year. That’s why – although the comet itself is nowhere near – Comet Halley is the parent of not just one, but two well-known annual meteor showers, one in May and one in October.

In early May, we see bits of this comet as the annual Eta Aquariid meteor shower.

Then, some six months later, in October, Earth in its orbit again intersects the orbital path of Comet Halley. This time around, these broken-up chunks from the comet burn up in Earth’s atmosphere as the annual Orionid meteor shower.

And, by the way, Halley is pronounced like valley. According to Ian Ridpath:

Many people nowadays say “Hailey,” a legacy of the 1950s rock group Bill Haley and the Comets.

Don’t miss the next spectacular sky event! Subscribe to EarthSky’s free daily newsletter for sky and science news.

The famous Halley’s Comet is the parent of 2 annual meteor showers: the Eta Aquariids in May and the Orionids in October. We witness these showers when we cross the comet’s orbit. But if we cross the orbit of Comet Halley twice each year, does that means there’s a chance that Earth and the comet will collide?

Comet debris litters Comet Halley’s orbit

Because Halley’s comet has circled the sun innumerable times over countless millennia, cometary fragments litter its orbit. That’s why the comet doesn’t need to be anywhere near the Earth or the sun in order to produce a meteor shower.

Instead, whenever our Earth in its orbit intersects Comet Halley’s orbit, cometary bits and pieces – often no larger than grains of sand or granules of gravel – smash into Earth’s upper atmosphere, to vaporize as fiery streaks across our sky: meteors.

The diagrams below can help you visualize Earth’s orbit with respect to the path of Halley’s comet.

Another view of Comet Halley’s orbit intersecting Earth’s

Their radiant points

You don’t need to know the radiant point to enjoy a meteor shower, because the meteors will appear anywhere in the sky, but if you trace back their direction, you’ll see that they seem to fly outward from one area. Meteor showers get their names from the location of the radiant point.

The Orionids radiate from a point near the upraised club of the constellation Orion the Hunter. And the Eta Aquariids appear to originate from the middle of Aquarius the Water Bearer.

Where is Comet Halley now?

Often, astronomers like to give distances of solar system objects in terms of astronomical units (AU). An AU is the sun-Earth distance. Halley’s comet lodges 0.587 AU from the sun at its closest point to the sun (perihelion) and 35.3 AU at its farthest point (aphelion).

In other words, at its farthest, Halley’s comet resides about 60 times farther from the sun than it does at its closest.

It was last at perihelion in 1986, and will again return to perihelion in 2061.

In December of 2023, the comet reached its farthest point from the sun that binds it in orbit. Then — pulled inexorably by the sun’s gravity — it curved around and is heading back toward the inner solar system again. Comet Halley will be back in 2061.

So the comet is far away. Even so, meteoroids — bits of debris left behind in the comet’s orbit — swim throughout Halley’s comet’s orbital stream. So each time Earth crosses the orbit of the comet, in May and October, these meteoroids turn into incandescent meteors once they plunge into the Earth’s upper atmosphere.

Meteor showers and comets

Of course, Halley’s comet isn’t the only comet that produces a major meteor shower.

Three of the comets in the table below are each responsible for two meteor showers. We’ve already discussed Halley’s comet. The asteroid 2004 TG10, responsible for the Northern Taurids, is part of the Taurid Complex, which includes Comet Encke, itself producing the Southern Taurids. And, asteroid 2003 EH1, responsible for the Quadrantids, appears to be part of the Machholz Complex, which also includes Comet 96P/Machholz, itself producing the Delta Aquariids.


What are those asteroids doing here?

Until recently a comet was a comet, and an asteroid was an asteroid. But the more we have learned about them the more the lines between them became blurred. The long-held belief that meteor showers can come only from active comets has been challenged by the discovery of asteroids being the parent objects of meteor showers. Most notably are the asteroids 2003 EH1 generating the Quadrantids and 3200 Phaethon behind the Geminids.

One of three things is going on here, or a combination of them. Perhaps the asteroid was once a comet and at that time expelled material that causes the meteor shower. The comet then became exhausted and all we have left is a small rocky nucleus.

Another possibility is that the asteroid was once part of a comet that at one time expelled material to cause the meteor shower, then the asteroid broke off and the comet was perturbed into a different orbit.

Or maybe the asteroid is still emitting material. A recent example of this is the asteroid Bennu, seen here ejecting material from its surface.

Bottom line: The famous Halley’s comet spawns the Orionid meteors in October and the Eta Aquariids in early May. It’ll return to the inner solar system in 2061. Other comets, and even some asteroids, produce meteor showers.

item.description:
• Japan plans to launch its MMX mission to Mars’ moons on October 19.
  • The spacecraft will explore Phobos and Deimos and collect a sample from Phobos.
  • The mission aims to return the sample to Earth in 2031.

MMX mission will travel to Phobos and bring a sample home

Japan is about to launch a new mission to Mars’ two moons, Phobos and Deimos, on October 19. Its main goal is to collect soil from Phobos and bring it back to Earth, where scientists hope it will reveal where the moons came from.

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) is preparing to launch its Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission from Tanegashima Space Center in Japan at 19:41 UTC (2:41 p.m. CDT) on October 19, 2026. That’s 4:41 a.m. Japan Standard Time on October 20.

After a journey of about 10 months, the spacecraft will reach Mars and its moons Phobos and Deimos. There, the mission will deploy a rover to land on and explore Phobos. After taking a sample of Phobos’ soil, it will return to Earth in 2031, depositing its precious cargo in Australia for retrieval.

Fascinating science, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter.

The 2 moons of Mars

Phobos — which means fear — and Deimos — which means terror — are the only two known moons of Mars, which takes its name from the Roman god of war. Astronomers long assumed these potato-shaped moons were captured asteroids that veered too close to Mars. However, astronomers have recently wondered if these nuggets are pieces of Mars that an impact flung into space. In fact, some think Phobos might once have been a ring around Mars … and it might one day break apart to become a ring once again.

How MMX will reach and sample Phobos

The components of the MMX mission

The MMX spacecraft has three parts. The propulsion module is what will get the spacecraft to Mars. Once there, the exploration module will visit Phobos’ surface with a rover and do soil sampling. Finally, the return module will journey back toward Earth and release a capsule that will target Australia.

Japan modeled the MMX mission after the highly successful Hayabusa2 mission that visited the asteroid Ryugu and returned samples to Earth. The Hayabusa2 mission discovered that Ryugu’s soil contained the building blocks of life.

We can’t wait to see what MMX discovers.

Bottom line: The MMX mission launches October 19 to explore Mars’ two moons. It will land on Phobos, collect a sample and bring it back to Earth in 2031.

item.title: Inferior conjunction — Venus! October 23-24, 2026 - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Venus in inferior conjunction

Venus travels one step inward from Earth in orbit around the sun. Its orbit is smaller than Earth’s. It has less distance to cover. And it moves faster in orbit (about 35 km/s or 78,300 mph in contrast to about 30 km/s or 67,000 mph for Earth). So – because Earth travels fast, too – Venus manages to gain a lap on us, going between us and the sun, about every 19.5 months. And, at such times, earthly astronomers say Venus is in inferior conjunction with the sun. Venus reaches inferior conjunction in 2026 at 4 UTC on Saturday, October 24, 2026. That’s 11 p.m. on October 23 CDT.

Will you see Venus on the day of inferior conjunction? It’s not likely, unless you’re an extremely careful and experienced telescopic and/or photographic observer. After all, on the day of inferior conjunction, Venus will be crossing the sky – as a slender crescent – with the sun during the day. And sometimes it’s closer to the sun than others. Please do not attempt to observe Venus near the sun unless you’re an experienced sun observer.

Venus moves to the morning sky

So, in a casual way, we say Venus goes between us and the sun on October 24, 2026. But it doesn’t go directly between. If it did, there’d be a transit of Venus. Venus – our closest planetary neighbor and the brightest planet in our sky – passes between the Earth and the sun about every 19 months (1.6 years). So inferior conjunction for Venus happens that often.

But transits of Venus are rare. And they happen in pairs. The last transits of Venus were on June 8, 2004 … and June 5-6, 2012. The previous pair of transits were in December 1874 and December 1882. The next transits of Venus will take place on December 10-11, 2117, and December 8, 2125.

The 2026 inferior conjunction of Venus

In 2026 – moving through the constellation Virgo the Maiden – Venus will pass south of the sun in our sky at the moment of inferior conjunction, at a distance of 6.6 degrees.

At the moment of inferior conjunction, Venus will officially shift from the evening to the morning sky for all observers on Earth.

When will you next see Venus?

So, when you can expect to see Venus come back to the morning sky? Around mid-month in November, look east about 20-30 minutes before sunrise. Since Venus is the brightest planet, you’ll be able to spot it low in the east, near the sunrise point, not long before the sun comes up. Venus will surprise you with its brightness so low in the sky! It’ll quickly become a bright morning “star” in November. In fact, by the middle of November, Venus will be heading for another greatest brilliancy around November 29.

Cycles of Venus

The 1.6-year period – after which the position of Venus relative to the sun repeats, as seen from Earth – is called its synodic period.

Notice that five synodic periods of Venus add up to eight years (just 2 1/2 days short). And so we have a cycle: inferior conjunctions of Venus that are eight years apart happen at the same time of year, in the same part of the sky, with Venus at a similar angular distance from the sun, that is, the same apparent distance from the sun on the sky’s dome. Over time, this 2 1/2-day variance will accumulate, so that the conjunctions “jump” into the previous month.

So inferior conjunctions of Venus strongly resemble each other on an 8-year cycle.

June transits of Venus

The June 3, 2020, passage of Venus nearly between us and the sun was quite dramatic. Venus appeared in our sky within “touching distance” of our star. Venus missed the solar disk in 2020 by only a quarter of a degree.

So, in 2020, Venus fell short of transiting, or crossing, the solar disk as it had done eight years earlier, on June 5, 2012 (and also eight years before that, on June 8, 2004).

With the conjunctions of 2004 and 2012 resulting in transits, and the one in 2020 resulting in a near-miss, one could correctly conclude that the angular distance from the sun during these (currently) June series of inferior conjunctions is slowly but steadily increasing. And so they are. The June-May inferior conjunctions of Venus will not result in any more transits for many centuries.

January transits of Venus

The last inferior conjunction on January 8-9, 2022, did not carry the drama of its predecessor in June 2020.

During the previous January inferior conjunction on January 10, 2014, Venus was around 1/3 of a degree farther from the sun than it was at the January 8-9, 2022, event. The next January conjunction, in 2030, will fall even closer than 2022, at just 4.5 degrees. So one might assume that this January series is slowly inching (in astronomical terms) towards the sun.

And that would be a correct assumption. Venus is currently getting closer and closer to the sun on the sky’s dome at the January inferior conjunctions.

What’s more, as the conjunction of 2022 fell on the 8th day of January, the 2 1/2 day shift will cause this January series to shift into December relatively soon, in 2045. From that moment, the now-December series will result in closer and closer approaches to the sun in the second half of the century and in the early 22nd century. The angular distance with the sun at the December inferior conjunction series will have decreased so much that it will bring us another pair of transits in years 2117 and 2125.

Some children alive today will likely live to see the Venus transits of the early 22nd century.

For experts, seeing Venus at inferior conjunction

Please do not attempt to observe Venus near the sun unless you’re an experienced sun observer.

Keen observers – depending on your location – might be able to see Venus through a telescope at – or near inferior conjunction – when it passes 6.6 degrees south of the sun on October 23-24, 2026. It’ll shine at -3.9 magnitude. And it’ll be a razor-thin crescent, only 61.12 arcseconds across.

To see a precise view from your location, try Stellarium Online.

One day before inferior conjunction – Venus in true color showing it has an atmosphere pic.twitter.com/RVmcFTQPoB

— Space Porn (@redditSpacePorn) January 9, 2022

Bottom line: Venus reaches inferior conjunction – passing between Earth and the sun – in 2026 at 4 UTC on October 24. Then Venus emerges in the morning sky.

item.title: Seeing Crescent Venus in Binoculars - Astroblog
item.description:
Venus in the twilight on Friday, October 16 as seen from Largs Pier at 20:08 ACST. Samsung S24, 5x Zoom, ISO 2000 1/33 sec exposureWestern sky on the evening of Saturday, October 17 as seen from Adelaide at 20:08 ACST (30 minutes after sunset, click to embiggen). Venus is just above the horizon and below Mercury. Venus is a clear thin "Crescent Moon" shape and is increasing in size. The shape is readily in 10x50 binoculars (although the brightness may make it hard to see due to internal lens reflections). 

The planets seen thorough binoculars are generally disappointing, Jupiter is a clear oblate spheroid, although featureless, but you can see the bright sparks of its satellites shuttling around. Saturn is a featureless ellipse, where you cant distinguish the rings from the planets body (but is is clearly an elliptical shape much boarder than Jupiter).

Very bad, cloud affected view of crescent Venus taken with my 10x50 binoculars and Samsung S24 on October 14, 20:00 ACDST.

But for the next few days you can easily see crescent Venus in 10x50 binoculars (and even to an extent in smaller binoculars).

The wire thin crescent shape is readily seen in 10x50 binoculars, although the brightness may make it hard to see due to internal lens reflections. Best seen close to twilight and with  a binocular stand or something to rest your arms on so the binoculars don't shake. 

You only have about 4 more days  until Venus disappears  into the twilight, but then by the 30th is is high enough above the eastern twilight horizon for the thin crescent to be seen in binoculars. 

So why not grab you binoculars and go have a look tonight?

item.title: Caves on the moon are target of new NASA mission - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
• NASA wants to search for caves on the moon. How will it search? And where?
  • A new mission named GIMLI will land and examine a volcanic pit — the Marius Hills Pit — in Oceanus Procellarum. It’s one of 300 such pits known on the moon.
  • GIMLI will use radar and other instruments to probe beneath the surface, looking for evidence of a lava tube-type cave.

Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter.

Searching for caves on the moon

Are there caves on the moon? We don’t know for sure yet, but evidence has been growing that they’re there.

Now, NASA has announced a new mission to search for moon caves. It’s called GIMLI for Geophysical Instruments for Marius Lunar pit Investigation. The plan is to land the mission at the volcanic Marius Hills Pit in Oceanus Procellarum (“Ocean of Storms”), a vast, dark lava plain or lunar mare (“sea”) located on the western edge of the moon’s near side.

NASA announced it had selected the new mission on September 30, 2026. Brooks Mendenhall described it in Astronomy magazine on October 9. An official targeted launch or arrival date for the GIMLI payload hasn’t yet been announced.

Fun fact: the mission is named after J.R.R. Tolkien’s cave-loving dwarf Gimli in The Lord of the Rings!

The Marius Hills Pit — often called the Marius Hills “hole” — is a steep-sided circular opening located within the Marius Hills volcanic region. GIMLI will peer down into the pit to see if it opens into a lava tube-type cave below the lunar surface. The pit is about 90 meters (295 feet) across. It’s approximately 50 meters (164 feet) deep.

And it could be a skylight, an opening in the roof of a lava tube, scientists believe.

On Earth, lava tubes form when the outer layer of a lava flow cools down while molten rock keeps moving beneath it. Later, the lava flow eventually stops. Then, when the lava drains away, it leaves behind a hollow channel or tunnel.

The mission was selected as part of the Payloads and Research Investigations on the Surface of the Moon (PRISM) program.

Science first

It will be exciting to see GIMLI land and to watch as it starts peering down into the pit. But the science will come first, according to Nicky Fox, associate administrator of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate. She said:

NASA Science is building the ultimate interplanetary survival guide to ensure that science goes first to the lunar surface to provide our future astronaut crews with the vital information, resources and safety precautions needed ahead of time to survive the night on the moon.

How GIMLI will search for caves on the moon

GIMLI won’t enter the pit itself. Instead, it’ll use a suite of instruments to scan below the surface.

For example, it’ll use the Norwegian Space Agency’s ground-penetrating radar. Plus, a gravimeter — a specialized scientific instrument used to measure local variations in a gravitational field — will help look for places in the pit where empty lava chambers might exist. And seismic sensors will measure sound waves moving through the ground. There will be cameras, too, of course.

Notably, this kind of subsurface scanning hasn’t been done on the lunar surface in decades. GIMLI’s principal investigator Than Putzig at the Planetary Science Institute said it:

… has essentially not been done since the Apollo astronauts.

That’s a long time, since the 1970s.

Why confirming a lava tube would be exciting

There are two reasons why confirming a lava tune on the moon would be exciting and important. Most intriguingly, it could offer protection to future astronauts. It could help shield them from the dangers of radiation from the sun, micro-meteoroids and extreme temperatures.

And for scientists, the planned GIMLI mission is an unprecedented opportunity to study a lava tube somewhere other than Earth. Scientists believe this moon cave would record the history of past volcanic activity on the moon. As Gareth Morgan at the Planetary Science Institute explained:

Confirming a substantial lava tube would give us an insight into how volcanism operated on the moon. Lava tubes are a common feature of basaltic volcanism on Earth, so identifying them on the moon means we could use knowledge of such terrestrial caves to better understand lunar history.

And even if GIMLI doesn’t find any caves, it could still determine how the pit formed. It would find more clues about the geologic and volcanic history of the moon overall.

What’s the evidence for lava tubes on the moon?

We know there are lava tubes on both Earth, Mars and Venus, so what about the moon?

Earthly lava tubes only get to about 100 feet (30 meters) across. But on the moon — with its weaker gravity — lava tubes might be larger. In fact, scientists estimate they could reach 1,260 feet (385 meters) across.

Scientists have found nearly 300 pits like Marius Hills Pit on the moon so far. Do any of them lead to subsurface lava tubes? These are the places to go when searching for caves on the moon.

NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter used radar to investigate one of those pits, in Mare Tranquillitatis, in 2024. The data suggested a possible lava tube about 100 feet long.

The Marius Hills Pit is another good contender. Radar data from the Kaguya orbiter plus gravity measurements from NASA’s GRAIL mission pointed strongly to a void beneath the surface.

Other PRISM selections

NASA officially released its first PRISM call for proposals on February 14, 2020. The other two PRISM selections include the Lunar Environment Monitoring Station – South Pole (LEMS-SP) and the Depth Imager with Spectral and Color Optics (DISCO).

LEMS-SP is an autonomous instrument suite. It is a a long-term environmental and hazard monitoring station. It will monitor falling micro-meteoroids and track the abundance of volatiles. Those are materials that can easily change into gas, that drift into the moon’s thin outer layer of gases.

Plus, it can also detect seismic activity, ie. moonquakes, with a short-period seismometer.

No, DISCO won’t play music on the moon. But it will search for ice below the surface in micro-cold traps. In addition, it will study how the lunar surface behaves, from how rocket exhaust disturbs the ground to how stable it is for mobility.

All of this will help NASA design the first moon base at the south pole. Fox said:

These PRISM selections will directly help NASA minimize risks to our astronauts while maximizing our agency goals as we set up humanity’s first lunar outpost in preparation for sending the first astronauts to Mars.

Bottom line: NASA is searching for caves on the moon. A new mission, GIMLI, will land at the volcanic Marius Hills Pit to look for a subsurface lava tube. Will it find one?

item.title: 2nd-generation planet: Was this world born around a dead star? - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
• Planets form in the disks of dust and gas around newborn stars. These are called 1st-generation planets. But there are 2nd-generation planets too. A 2nd-generation planet can form in the material cast off from dead white dwarf stars.
  • Astronomers might have found a 2nd-generation planet around the white dwarf HS 0209+0832. It is in archives from the Hubble Space Telescope.
  • A “cold case” mystery about the white dwarf might now be solved thanks to the discovery.

Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter.

Astronomers detect possible 2nd-generation planet

Planets typically form from the huge disks of dust and gas around newborn stars. These are what scientists call 1st-generation planets. But our universe evolves. So it should also contain 2nd-generation planets. A 2nd-generation planet is one that formed in material cast off from a dead star.

Now, for the first time, astronomers have detected a possible 2nd-generation planet that formed around a white dwarf. That is, the dense core left over by a dying star. They detected this planet in the data archive of the Hubble Space Telescope.

The potential discovery might solve an old “cold case” mystery about this white dwarf, which is named HS 0209+0832. Scientists have known for some time that this white dwarf has an unusually high amount of the element niobium in its atmosphere. And they’ve wondered … why? This phoenix-like planet rising from the dead star’s ashes might be the answer.

The researchers published their peer-reviewed paper in Nature Astronomy on October 5, 2026.

1st chapter of a long tale

We tend to think that after a star dies — probably along with its planets — that that’s it. But it’s not necessarily the end of the story. Astronomer Jamie Williams is the lead author of the new study at the University of Warwick in the U.K. He said:

Rather than the white dwarf stage being a kind of epilogue to the story of a star and its planets, this research points to the systems we are familiar with only being the first chapter of a potentially much longer tale, with some new characters showing up. That’s a really exciting prospect to pursue.

He added:

The 2nd-generation planets are worlds that form out of the material a star casts off as it dies. They’re incredibly rare, and finding one around a white dwarf was completely unexpected. It’s a bit like finding a planet that has risen from the ashes of the very star it once orbited.

Unknown chemical signatures

Ever since Hubble first observed HS 0209+0832 in 1999, a mystery has shrouded the white dwarf. Hubble detected about 100 chemical signatures that couldn’t be identified.

At the time, they remained unknown. But now, the researchers have used an updated chemical database. They found that the element niobium could explain many of these detections. And there was a lot of it. Williams said:

What Hubble is showing us in this white dwarf system is something we haven’t seen before: a high abundance of the element niobium, the signature of which I was unfamiliar with when I first found it in the archival data.

Niobium points to a 2nd-generation planet

The amount of niobium is also a clue. It suggested the presence of a planet that formed after the original star had died and became a white dwarf: a 2nd-generation planet. Co-author Nicholas Stone, a theoretical astrophysicist at the University of Wisconsin – Madison, said:

Niobium and other elements heavier than iron are astronomically special because, unlike many common elements, they are not formed in the cores of stars by thermonuclear fusion. Instead, these heavy elements can only be synthesized in the exotic conditions that briefly emerge inside dying stars. The presence of niobium is a signpost of these ‘death’ throes, and the expulsion of the dying star’s innards into space.

This pattern of elements is a telltale sign of the ‘s-process,’ a nuclear reaction that builds heavy elements inside dying stars during their bloated red giant phase. It’s a chemical signature no ordinary, ‘1st-generation’ planet should carry, which told us that this new planet was something different.

This is the first time that scientists have detected niobium in the atmosphere of a white dwarf, as co-author Boris Gaensicke, also at the University of Warwick, noted:

When Jamie asked me about niobium in relation to this study I was truly gobsmacked, as that element had not been reported in any other white dwarf analyzed to date. Once we realized it was there, everything fell into place.

What kind of planet is it?

The researchers estimate the planet itself to be about the size of Jupiter, therefore a gas giant. But it is quickly losing its atmosphere. Why is that?

The researchers say it is because the white dwarf is still very hot and bombarding the planet with intense radiation. Not surprising, since the planet orbits only 3.7 million miles (6 million kilometers) from the white dwarf. That’s a lot closer than Mercury is from the sun, at 36 million miles (58 million kilometers).

In fact, the planet might have a comet-like tail of material. This material would then fall back onto the white dwarf. That’s why the niobium is in the atmosphere of the white dwarf. And notably, Mercury also has a tail, of sodium.

Even though the white dwarf planet is losing its atmosphere, it will likely survive for a long time yet, as Williams noted:

If the 2nd-generation planet is there, I think it is likely to survive. Eventually the white dwarf will cool and then maintain a consistent temperature, with the planet in its stable habitable zone for millions of years.

A companion star?

The researchers also think that the white dwarf might have had a companion star. Williams said:

Forming the protoplanetary disc in this situation is not easy and helps explain why these planets are so rare. A single, isolated star dies and sheds mass in a roughly symmetrical way. To form a disc of material necessary to birth a planet, HS 0209+0832 likely required a companion star that pulled the ejected material back into orbit, rather than letting it escape.

Data about the 2nd-generation planet from other missions

Two other missions also provided additional data that support the existence of the 2nd-generation planet. These are NASA’s now-retired FUSE (Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer) and NASA’s TESS (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite).

FUSE corroborated the findings of large amounts of niobium in the white dwarf system. And TESS observed the system for four straight months. It detected periodic variations in brightness of the white dwarf. These variations are evidence for a planet that orbits at only 3.7 million miles (6 million kilometers) from the white dwarf.

The HS 0209+0832 system will provide valuable data about white dwarfs and any planets that still exist around them. As Gaensicke said:

I think this research is an important example of the fact that scientific discovery is not a straight path. It often needs that magical moment when people discuss big questions on their minds and realize that together they can find unexpected answers.

Bottom line: Astronomers might have found a new 2nd-generation planet orbiting a white dwarf star. It could also help answer a “cold case” mystery about the white dwarf.

item.title: Space is getting crowded. Here’s the latest satellite report - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Earth orbit is getting more crowded, and the consequences could be serious. The European Space Agency’s 2026 Space Environment Report warns that debris collisions could trigger a runaway chain reaction, making some orbital regions unsafe or unusable. Space hazards expert Jonathan McDowell joins EarthSky to explain what the report reveals, how dangerous conditions in space have become, and what we can do about it. Watch in the player above.

Science news, the night sky and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter

Space is getting crowded. Let’s look at the numbers

In September 2026, ESA’s Space Debris Office published its annual Space Environment Report. And, as you might suspect, the news is that space — in particular low Earth orbit — is getting more crowded. Here’s a look at the basic numbers as of October 2026 from OrbitalRadar.com:

  • 31,000+ total tracked objects in low Earth orbit
  • 18,600+ payloads in orbit, working and nonworking
  • 15,800+ of those are working satellites
  • 10,000+ of the working satellites are Starlink

And, according to ESA, the only place those numbers are going to go is up. ESA, which based its report on data through 2025, outlined some of the biggest concerns:

  • The number and scale of commercial satellite constellations continue to increase each year.  
  • Not enough satellites leave heavily congested orbits at the end of their lives, creating a growing collision risk. The expected number of objects and collisions in low-Earth orbit are skyrocketing in a runaway effect. (Read more: The Kessler syndrome) 
  • More than three intact satellites or rocket bodies are reentering every day. Plus, 10 new payloads are launched daily. (Read more: 1 to 2 Starlink satellites are falling back to Earth each day)
  • In 2026, ESA added an on-ground casualty risk of reentries. While the risk is still very low, the chance is still increasing every year due to increased traffic.  

Let’s visualize the numbers

Here are some graphics from ESA to help us visualize the numbers of satellites in orbit and being added to orbit.

The pluses and minuses of reentry

Because there are now so many satellites in low Earth orbit, it’s important that they get removed from orbit when they’ve reached the end of their lives. And one of the positive findings of ESA’s 2026 report was that there are more controlled reentries now. That means companies and governments are conducting planned end-of-life disposal of their satellites.

But reentries have drawbacks. As they burn up in our atmosphere, they deposit heavy metals. There are many issues this deposit could lead to, include damaging the ozone layer, affecting the climate and altering the atmosphere’s natural chemistry.

And then, of course, there’s the new metric ESA introduced this year: the risk of casualties on the ground. While you are still much more likely to be injured or killed in a car or on a staircase, the risk of harm from satellite reentry has naturally gone up as the number of reentering satellites goes up. More controlled reentries would help to mitigate this risk.

Space is getting crowded: What are the real risks?

The biggest immediate concern, as we send more and more satellites into low Earth orbit, is that the rising population seems unstoppable. That is, until collisions cascade into more collisions and make the environment unusable.

This idea that satellites will collide and create debris that produces more collisions until we have a runaway cascading effect is called the Kessler syndrome.

As recently as October 5, 2026, LeoLabs detected a satellite breakup in a crowded low-Earth environment. LeoLabs spotted multiple objects near the inactive Meteor 2-7 satellite after it passed over a radar station in Western Australia. Followup observations from other radars confirmed that a debris-generating event occurred. The company called it a:

… worrying trend for space safety and security.

But ESA — along with other space organizations — is working on ways to reduce the risk. This will involve cleaning up orbits and working toward a zero debris solution.

Bottom line: ESA has put out an annual report documenting the state of low Earth orbit. The number of satellites in orbit is skyrocketing, along with the chance for collisions and on-ground casualties.

item.title: Planetary systems fall into 2 distinct families, astronomers say - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter.

Planetary systems fall into 2 distinct families

Astronomers from the International Space Science Institute said on October 13, 2026, that planetary systems appear to fall into one of two families depending on their home star. After studying 300 of the best-characterized planetary systems in the Milky Way galaxy, they found that less massive stars tend to form planetary systems that are smaller in mass and width but with more planets. On the other hand, more massive stars tend to form planetary systems that are more chaotic and wider with more massive, though fewer, planets.

The researchers published their study in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Astronomy on October 13, 2026.

The 2 types of families

The researchers said that a planetary system’s host star appears to determine how its planets form and evolve. The amount of material in the cloud of gas and dust that forms the star influences what type of planetary family results. Let’s take a closer look at the two family types.

The compact planetary system

The compact, lower-mass planetary systems tend to orbit stars that are as massive as or less massive than our sun. These stars also tend to have similar or lower amounts of heavy elements. The width of the planetary system is smaller and it has less massive planets, but they’re packed more tightly. But not everything about this family type is diminutive. It tends to have more planets than the more massive planetary system.

Scientists said the lower-mass systems have neighboring planets that are similar to each other, or what they call “peas in a pod.” These systems have less gravitational upheaval and more orderly systems. To sum up:

  • Host stars are as massive as or less massive than our sun, with similar or lower amounts of heavy elements
  • Planets are less massive and more similar to each other
  • Orbits are compact, close to the host star
  • Dynamic history is less violent and closer to our solar system

The wider planetary system

The wider planetary systems have stars that are more massive than our sun. These stars have a higher proportion of heavy elements. This results in planets that are more massive, though fewer in number. However, these larger worlds orbiting their stars can gravitationally interact, causing instabilities. So the planets that survive these interactions are more likely to have varied orbits. To sum up this family:

  • Host stars are more massive than our sun, with more heavy elements
  • Planets are fewer but more massive
  • Orbits are wider and more varied
  • Dynamic history is violent with possible collisions and ejections

So why are wider systems unstable?

The wider planetary systems are more violent and chaotic, with planetary collisions and ejections. These processes can leave planets in a variety of orbits. Danae Polychroni, of the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics, explained why:

The scenarios that best reproduce the dynamical properties of the family of wide and massive systems are those in which the systems are unstable from birth. The greater abundance of material from which planets form around their host stars causes them to be born too large, preventing the system from remaining stable.

Sorting planetary systems

Co-author Diego Turrini of the International Space Science Institute said:

The fundamental question we started from was: What determines the characteristics of planetary systems as we see them today? Are they established at birth or sculpted by evolution over time? The truth, in the end, turned out to lie somewhere in the middle. Our results show that there is a genetic link between planetary systems and their stars, and that, depending on the star around which they are born, this link also determines their fate.

Co-author Camilla Danielski of the University of Valencia said:

The main difficulty during the data analysis was determining whether the two families of planetary systems were real or just an illusion created by the technological limits of current observational techniques. At the end of the path, it became clear that selection effects acted as the tip of the iceberg, revealing the existence of much deeper structural diversities between these systems.

The astronomers hope that understanding which stars create which planetary systems will help in the search for planets that could be home to life.

Bottom line: Astronomers studying planetary systems in the Milky Way have found they can be sorted into two families. These families are largely determined by the host star.

Source: Two families of multi-planet systems with distinct architectures and stellar hosts

item.title: What star in the northeast flashes colorfully? It’s Capella! - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
You deserve a daily dose of good news. For the latest in science and the night sky, subscribe to EarthSky’s free daily newsletter.

Capella is the colorful, twinkling star in the northeast

This evening, check out one of the flashiest stars in the sky. It’s the brightest star in the northeast this month. It’s so bright that every year in northern autumn, we get questions from people in the Northern Hemisphere who see a star twinkling with colorful flashes. It lies low in the northeastern sky in early evening as seen from mid-northern locations. That star is Capella.

The reason it’s so flashy is because it’s a bright star shining near the horizon. That means its light is coming to us through our thick atmosphere. The wavering air makes its point of light jump around, split into colors and appear to flash.

If you could travel to it in space, you’d find that Capella is really two golden stars, both with roughly the same surface temperature as our local star, the sun … but both larger and brighter.

Capella is in the constellation Auriga the Charioteer. Since antiquity, Capella’s nickname has been the Goat Star. You might pick it out just by gazing northeastward from a Northern Hemisphere latitude during the evening hours in October. Capella climbs upward throughout the night, and this month soars high overhead in the wee hours before dawn.

Why stars twinkle or flash

So, Capella is a golden point of light that flashes red, green and blue when it’s low in the sky. Why does it do that?

The reality is that every star in the sky undergoes the same process as Capella when it twinkles. That is, every star’s light must shine through Earth’s atmosphere before reaching our eyes. But not every star flashes as noticeably as Capella. The flashes happen because Capella is low in the sky in the evening at this time of the year. And, when you look at an object low in the sky, you’re looking through more atmosphere than when the same object is overhead.

The atmosphere splits or refracts the star’s light, just as a prism splits sunlight.

So that’s where Capella’s red, green and blue flashes are coming from — not from the star itself, but from the refraction of its light by our atmosphere. When you see Capella higher in the sky, you’ll find that these glints of color will disappear.

By the way, why are these flashes of color so especially noticeable with Capella? The reason is simply that it’s a very bright star. It’s the sixth brightest star in Earth’s sky, not including our sun.

Here are 2 other flashing stars of autumn

If the flashy star you’re seeing doesn’t seem to be Capella (wrong time, wrong location), here are a couple of other options. Arcturus is in the northwest at this time of year. Follow the curving handle of the Big Dipper toward the horizon, and if it hits the star you’re wondering about, then you’re looking at Arcturus in Boötes.

Another option is Sirius. If you’re waking before dawn this time of the year, you’ll find Sirius toward the south. Check out the maps below to see which star is twinkling at you.

Bottom line: If you’re in Earth’s Northern Hemisphere and see a bright star twinkling with red, green and blue flashes low in the northeast on October evenings, it’s probably Capella. See charts here!

item.title: Tiny Gold Nanogaps Could Crack the Chirality Puzzle - Universe Today
item.description: Looking for biosignatures across the solar system requires looking for asymmetry. Amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, are famously either “left-handed” (L) or “right-handed” (D). We know abiotic processes (i.e. those that create amino acids but don’t involve life) create a 50/50 mixture of the two types, which is called a racemic mixture. But life as we know it almost exclusively relies on left-handed amino acids to fold proteins and right-handed ones to construct nucleic acids. So if we find an imbalance in the types of amino acids we analyze from somewhere in the solar system, it's a good indication that life is behind that imbalance. Differentiating between the two “chiralities”, as they’re called, is possible, but typically requires advanced equipment and chemical disposables that make them burdensome for spaceflight applications. But a new paper in Nature Communications from researchers led by Takahito Ohshiro and Masateru Taniguchi of Osaka University offers an alternative - a solid-state quantum tunneling sensor that can read the chirality of a single amino acid molecule using basically just some gold wire.

item.title: NASA’s Perseverance rover on Mars sets off-world driving record - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
You deserve a daily dose of good news. For the latest in science and the night sky, subscribe to EarthSky’s free daily newsletter.

Congratulations, Perseverance rover!

As of October 11, 2026, NASA’s Perseverance rover has driven 28.10 miles (45.22 km) on Mars. That’s a new off-world driving record for total distance driven by any vehicle on the surface of another world. The previous record of 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers) was held by NASA’s Opportunity rover. Perseverance reached that mark on the 2,006th Martian day, or sol, of its mission. NASA said;

It covered in five and a half years a distance that took Opportunity almost 15.

The six-wheeled geologist has in less than six years surpassed a mark set by the agency’s Opportunity rover, which explored the Red Planet for nearly 15 years.

The milestone came as Perseverance traveled toward an area called Idubi through the region off the western rim of Jezero Crater nicknamed Lac de Charmes. There, the rover is investigating what may be some of the oldest terrain ever explored in the solar system.

The rocks and terrain of Lac de Charmes are so ancient that their Earthly equivalents have long since been erased by erosion and plate tectonics. But Mars doesn’t have tectonic plates. And Idubi is where the science team hopes to find traces of ancient hydrothermal (heated water) systems.

Humans set goals, Perseverance self-drives

Much of the credit belongs to Perseverance’s self-driving capability, NASA said. Using an autonomous navigation system known as AutoNav, the rover images the terrain while rolling, builds a 3D map of hazards, and plots its course between waypoints selected by rover planners on Earth — a capability the team calls thinking while driving.

Perseverance can do all that at or near its top speed, covering as much as 1,351 feet (412 meters) in a single sol.

The six-wheeled scientist has driven more than 90% of its total distance using AutoNav to evaluate the terrain. That’s in contrast to about 5% for the first Martian AutoNav system on Opportunity and its twin, Spirit. Where NASA’s first Mars rover, Sojourner, assessed the path ahead using 20 measurement points, Perseverance processes 600,000 with every look.

Steven Lee, the project manager of the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, said:

It is an honor to be working on Perseverance at a moment when the technology has evolved to the point that drives like these are routine. The original mission called for no more than 12.4 miles of driving. We’ve blown well past that, and with all mobility systems fully operational and favorable extended-ground-life test results, we expect Perseverance to keep adding to this record for many years to come.

NASA recently approved the mission’s first extension, which began in October and will carry Perseverance’s exploration of the crater rim through roughly the end of 2028.

3 decades of Mars rovers

Perseverance’s record caps nearly three decades of NASA rover operations on Mars, each mission driving farther and more capably than the last.

The microwave-oven-size Sojourner rover covered about 330 feet (100 meters) during its 83-sol mission in 1997. The golf-cart-size twins Spirit and Opportunity arrived in 2004 with 90-sol prime missions. Spirit logged 4.8 miles (7.7 km) before succumbing to the Martian winter in 2010. Opportunity kept rolling for 5,111 sols, completing the first extraterrestrial marathon in 2015 and setting the record Perseverance has now surpassed. The agency’s Curiosity rover, which landed in Gale Crater in 2012 and remains hard at work, has logged more than 23.65 miles (38.07 kilometers).

Mark Maimone, deputy team chief for robotic operations on Perseverance, said:

The rover that broke this record did so by making its own decisions about the path. Given the autonomy to just go, Perseverance is a better driver than the one that landed, and we’re not done,

Our newest software teaches Perseverance to steer less and roll more, and to check its own position against orbital maps mid-drive.

The next frontier is sunlight itself. Glare in the navigation cameras is why we park by mid-afternoon if we’re driving toward the sun, and if we can teach the rover to see past those artifacts, every rover that follows gets a longer working day.

Not just Mars, and why it matters

The extraterrestrial off-road driving record isn’t limited to Mars: Lunar driving records were broken earlier in the journey. Perseverance rolled past both the 22.2 miles (35.7 kilometers) covered by Apollo 17 astronauts Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt in 1972 and the 24.2 miles (39 kilometers) driven by the Soviet Union’s Lunokhod 2 rover in 1973.

Setting distance records is just a bonus. Stamina and longer drives are putting more geologic diversity within reach faster — more outcrops examined and more of the Red Planet’s history read from its rocks. That reach carried Perseverance from an ancient lakebed up a fossilized river system, where the rover found a potential biosignature at a rock called Cheyava Falls, and on to the crater rim, where an entirely different kind of ancient habitat — hydrothermal (heated water) — may await.

Perseverance has collected 29 rock and regolith samples. The samples span the crater floor, a delta fan formed by a long-gone river, and now the crater rim. In the latter region, it has been exploring impact-generated rocks some 4 billion years old. On Earth, that chapter of planetary history has been almost entirely erased.

After Lac de Charmes, the rover will continue along the crater rim and head south during the extended mission towards Rainbow Falls, a 328-foot-wide (100-meter-wide) block of ancient crust uplifted by the impact that created Jezero.

Bottom line: The Mars Perseverance rover has set a new distance record on Mars. It has driven 28.10 miles (45.22 km). Perseverance reached that mark on October 11, 2026, the 2,006th Martian day, or sol, of its mission.
